title: Algebraic Expressions and Polynomials — Class 10 NIOS Mathematics
subject: Mathematics

slides.title: Algebraic Expressions and Polynomials
bullets: Class 10 — NIOS Mathematics
Chapter 3
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. In this lesson we tighten our grip on algebraic vocabulary, then meet the special class of expressions called polynomials and learn to add, subtract, multiply and evaluate them.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Identify variables, constants, terms, coefficients in any expression.
Combine like terms; classify by number of terms.
Decide if an expression is a polynomial; find its degree and standard form.
Add, subtract and multiply polynomials.
Evaluate a polynomial at a number; check if a value is a zero.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each objective; ask students which they feel least sure about and weight the lesson accordingly.

slides.title: Vocabulary — variable, constant, term, coefficient
bullets: Variable: a letter that stands for a number (x, y, p…).
Constant: a fixed number (3, −7, √2).
Term: a part separated from others by + or −.
Coefficient: the numerical factor of a term, with sign.
Constant term: a term with no variable part (just a number).
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through 5p^3 − 2p^2 + p − 9 on the board: 4 terms, with coefficients 5, −2, 1 and constant term −9.

slides.title: Like terms and combining them
bullets: Like terms have the same variable part.
7x^2 and −4x^2 are like; 7x^2 and 7x are unlike.
Combine like terms by adding/subtracting their coefficients.
Unlike terms cannot be combined this way.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress that 'same variable part' means same letter AND same exponents. This is the workhorse rule for the entire chapter.

slides.title: Classifying by number of terms
bullets: Monomial — exactly one term: 5x, −7p^3, 2/3.
Binomial — two unlike terms: 3x + 5, p^2 − 7p.
Trinomial — three unlike terms: x^2 + 3x − 2.
Multinomial — more than three.
Combine like terms first before counting.
slides.speaker_notes: Quick whip-round: ask the class to classify 2x + 3 + 5x — answer: binomial 7x + 3, not trinomial.

slides.title: What is a polynomial?
bullets: Two rules: (i) only non-negative integer powers, (ii) no variable in any denominator.
Polynomials: 7, 3x + 5, x^2 − 4x + 4, 2y^3 − y + 6.
NOT polynomials: 3/x, √x, x^(−2) + 5, 2/(x + 1).
Constants like 7 ARE polynomials (degree 0).
Both rules must hold; one violation is enough to disqualify.
slides.speaker_notes: Use the card-sort cards from Explore. The big surprise for many students is that 7 is a polynomial.

slides.title: Degree of a polynomial
bullets: One variable: largest exponent (e.g. 5z^4 + z^2 − 1 has degree 4).
Several variables: largest sum-of-exponents across terms.
For 4xy + 7x^2 y^3: term degrees are 1+1=2 and 2+3=5; polynomial degree is 5.
Names: 0 = constant, 1 = linear, 2 = quadratic, 3 = cubic, 4 = biquadratic.
Standard form: terms in descending order of degree.
slides.speaker_notes: Before clicking each bullet, ask students to pre-compute the degree.

slides.title: Worked example: add (3x^2 − 5x + 2) + (x^2 + 7x − 6)
bullets: Group like terms: (3x^2 + x^2) + (−5x + 7x) + (2 − 6).
x^2 terms: 4x^2.
x terms: 2x.
Constants: −4.
slides.speaker_notes: Show the same problem in vertical layout side-by-side. Students copy the version they prefer.

slides.title: Subtraction = flip signs, then add
bullets: To subtract a polynomial, change the sign of every term, then add.
The result is again a polynomial.
Degree(sum or diff) ≤ max(deg p, deg q) (can drop if leading terms cancel).
slides.speaker_notes: Common slip: forgetting to flip signs of the inner terms — only the leading sign. Walk slowly.

slides.title: Multiplying — distributive law
bullets: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Every term of the first × every term of the second.
Monomial × polynomial: 3x^2(2x + 5) = 6x^3 + 15x^2.
Binomial × binomial: FOIL — First, Outer, Inner, Last.
Long × long: vertical long-multiplication.
slides.speaker_notes: Big idea: multiplication is just distribution applied repeatedly. FOIL is a memorisable subset for binomial × binomial.

slides.title: FOIL: (x + 2)(x + 3)
bullets: First: x · x = x^2.
Outer: x · 3 = 3x.
Inner: 2 · x = 2x.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress the combine-like-terms step at the end (3x + 2x = 5x). Students often forget to combine.

slides.title: Vertical multiplication: (2x^2 − 3x + 1)(x − 4)
bullets: Degree(product) = 3 = 2 + 1 = deg p + deg q.
slides.speaker_notes: Note the degree rule: adding degrees is one of the most useful sanity checks for polynomial arithmetic.

slides.title: Evaluating a polynomial; zeros
bullets: p(a) is the number obtained by replacing x with a and simplifying.
A zero (root) of p is an x with p(x) = 0.
For p(x) = x^2 − 4x + 4, p(2) = 4 − 8 + 4 = 0, so x = 2 is a zero.
A degree-n polynomial has at most n zeros (with multiplicity).
slides.speaker_notes: Foreshadow the chapters on linear and quadratic equations: finding zeros is exactly the work of those chapters.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 1. Classify 4xy + 7x^2 y^3 by number of terms; state its degree.
2. Subtract (2y^2 − 3y + 5) from (5y^2 + y − 1).
3. Expand (x − 4)(x + 6) using FOIL.
4. Verify whether x = 1 is a zero of p(x) = x^3 − 1.
Compare answers with your bench partner.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk the room. Watch for students who try to FOIL but forget to combine like terms — common slip.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. How many terms in 3x^2 + 5x − 7?
Q2. Coefficient of x^2 in −x^2 + 4?
Q3. Is x^(−2) + 1 a polynomial?
Q4. Degree of (x + 1)(x^2 − 3)?
Show your answers on fingers (1 = first option …).
slides.speaker_notes: Use show-of-fingers to gauge the room without singling anyone out. Address the question with the most disagreement.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Variable / constant / term / coefficient — the four-word vocabulary.
Polynomial = whole-number powers + no variable in denominator.
Degree = max exponent (1 var) or max sum-of-exponents (many vars).
Add/subtract by combining like terms; subtraction flips signs first.
Multiply by distributing; FOIL for binomials, vertical for long polynomials.
Evaluate by substitution; a zero is an x making p(x) = 0.
slides.speaker_notes: End with the 6 takeaways. Hand out the worksheet and announce the homework prompts.
